name: Political unitarism
summary: Political unitarism advocates a fully unified, centralised system of government in which one central authority holds supreme power and regions have no entrenched self-rule. It aims to move powers from federal units, autonomous regions or cantons to the centre, producing a unitary state with a single legislature. It is a doctrine about territorial structure and takes no stance on economic, social or cultural questions.
scope: Unitarism as a general doctrine of territorial centralisation, drawn from the Wikipedia articles on political unitarism and the unitary state, Alexander Hamilton's 1787 Convention speech favouring a complete national sovereignty, the Argentine Unitarian Party's centralist programme, and Gerring and Thacker's comparative study. It excludes the religious Unitarianism and the Argentine party's wider liberal programme except where noted.

missingStatements.rationale: The article on political unitarism says regional powers are not entrenched in the constitution so the centre can reduce or abolish them.

missingStatements.text: A country should have one legislature with exclusive lawmaking power over its whole territory.
missingStatements.rationale: A single legislature with exclusive power over the whole territory is named as a practical aim of unitarism, and Hamilton argued two sovereignties cannot coexist.
missingStatements.declined: Same unitarist principle as regional-powers-revocable (one sovereign legislature); covered there, and adding it would make the bank redundant.

missingStatements.text: The national government should be able to appoint or override the heads of regional governments.
missingStatements.rationale: Hamilton's 1787 sketch had each state's governor appointed by the general government, and the unitary-state article says prefects represent the state in each department.
missingStatements.declined: Appointing regional heads is one mechanism of the same central control, held at weak value 1; covered by regional-powers-revocable.
